'The Lord is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?'
The bodies of the Yom Kippur sin offerings burned outside the camp.
'Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving.'

misread.popular: Hebrews 13:8 is quoted as a stand-alone slogan, for example to argue that all New Testament miracles must happen today in the same way.
misread.better: In context it ties together remembering faithful leaders (Heb 13:7) and resisting strange teachings (Heb 13:9): the Jesus they preached is the same Jesus now, so stay with him. It is about faithfulness to the original gospel, not a ruling on spiritual gifts.

misreadings.topic: 'Obsolete': does Hebrews say Judaism has been replaced?
misreadings.popular: Hebrews 8:13 shows that God has finished with the Jewish religion. The old covenant was a failed system of rituals, the Jews are no longer God's covenant people, and the church has taken Israel's place.
misreadings.inContext: The 'new covenant' is not a Christian invention but a promise God made to 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah' through Jeremiah (Jer 31:31-34). Hebrews quotes it as Israel's own hope now fulfilled in the Messiah. The fault named is 'with them' (Heb 8:8), the people's unfaithfulness, exactly as Jeremiah himself said, not with Torah as God's gift. What is 'near to vanishing' is the first covenant's system of priesthood and sacrifice as the means of access, which the author sees as provisional and pointing ahead. Richard Hays describes Hebrews as a form of Jewish sectarian 'new covenantalism', comparable to how the Qumran community saw itself as the people of a renewed covenant, and argues it is not a statement of Christianity over Judaism. Mark Nanos pushes further to 'renewed covenantalism'. Pamela Eisenbaum, a Jewish scholar, has argued that Hebrews is not about Jews and Christians as separate religions at all, since that division did not yet exist. Hebrews never mentions the Pharisees, never accuses Jews of legalism, and holds up Israel's saints as the church's own ancestors (Heb 11).
misreadings.defence: Careful evangelical scholars such as F. F. Bruce, George Guthrie and Thomas Schreiner agree that 'legalistic Jews' caricatures are foreign to Hebrews and that the new covenant is Israel's promise. They nonetheless argue that Hebrews really does claim a decisive discontinuity: the Levitical priesthood and its sacrifices cannot perfect the conscience (Heb 10:1-4), and after Christ there is no return to them. Schreiner holds that Hebrews teaches that the old covenant as a covenant has been fulfilled and set aside. Most agree, however, that 'set aside because fulfilled' is different from 'God rejected the Jewish people', and Hebrews says nothing about the latter.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Supersessionist readings of Hebrews were used historically to justify contempt and violence toward Jews. Reading 8:13 inside Jeremiah's promise keeps the strong Christology of Hebrews without turning it into anti-Judaism.

misreadings.topic: Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26: can a Christian lose salvation?
misreadings.popular: Two opposite popular readings exist. Some take these verses as proof that a believer can lose salvation and then can never get it back. Others, defending 'once saved, always saved', say the people described were never truly saved, only close to faith, or that the 'punishment' is loss of rewards, not of salvation.
misreadings.inContext: In a covenant setting, apostasy means publicly breaking loyalty with one's patron and benefactor. David deSilva reads 6:4-8 in patron-client terms: to repudiate the Son after receiving his gifts is to shame the benefactor publicly ('holding him up to contempt', Heb 6:6), the worst ingratitude imaginable, and there is no other broker to turn to. The descriptions (enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit) are the author's normal words for genuine Christian experience. Scot McKnight's influential 1992 study read all five warnings together and concluded that the audience is believers, the sin is apostasy, and the consequence is final judgment. The point is pastoral: the warning is a fence at a cliff edge meant to keep people from going over, and the author immediately adds 'we are persuaded better things of you' (Heb 6:9).
misreadings.defence: Reformed scholars answer in several ways. Thomas Schreiner and Ardel Caneday (The Race Set Before Us) agree with McKnight that the audience is believers and the threat is real eternal judgment, but argue the warnings are the very means God uses to keep his elect persevering, so a true believer heeds them and does not fall. Others (following John Owen, and in some form Wayne Grudem) argue the experiences described fall short of regeneration, comparing them to the wilderness generation who saw God's works yet did not believe. Arminian and Wesleyan readers take the text to describe a real possibility of falling away. These are serious scholarly positions, not popular errors; what popular preaching often misses is that Hebrews is aimed at a weary community under social pressure, not at troubled individuals worried about a single sin.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The passages have caused real anguish to sensitive believers who fear they have committed an unforgivable sin. Read in context, they warn against deliberate, public repudiation of Jesus, and they are addressed to people the preacher believes will persevere.

misreadings.topic: Hebrews 11 as a 'faith hall of fame'
misreadings.popular: Hebrews 11 is a list of spiritual giants whose great faith we should admire and imitate, each a stand-alone example of believing hard enough for God to act.
misreadings.inContext: Hebrews 11 is part of a sermon whose 'therefore' comes in 12:1: these people are a 'cloud of witnesses' surrounding runners in a stadium, and the point is endurance toward Jesus. Most of the faith described is faithfulness under uncertainty and shame: Abraham leaving without knowing where, Moses choosing reproach, people tortured and homeless (Heb 11:35-38). Many did not receive what was promised (Heb 11:13; Heb 11:39). Pamela Eisenbaum showed that, unlike typical Jewish hero lists (Sir 44-50, 1 Maccabees 2), Hebrews chooses figures who stand somewhat outside national institutions, people who were marginal, wandering and unsettled. They model the community's own condition. The list ends 'apart from us they should not be made perfect': the ancestors and the church form one family completed together.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical commentators such as F. F. Bruce, George Guthrie and Thomas Schreiner agree fully that chapter 11 must be read with 12:1-3 and is about persevering faith, not heroic achievement. Popular devotional use that celebrates individual heroes is not wrong to admire them, since Hebrews does say 'the world was not worthy' of them (Heb 11:38), but it loses the call to endurance under shame. This is a case of popular flattening, not scholarly disagreement.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Read as a hall of fame, the chapter can make faith sound like a spiritual superpower. Read as the sermon intends, it comforts people who are suffering and have not yet seen God's promises fulfilled.

misreadings.popular: Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as believing in what you cannot see, often in contrast to evidence or reason; faith is a strong inner certainty.
misreadings.inContext: The key words are hypostasis (substance, assurance, the 'reality' that underlies something) and elenchos (proof, conviction). Faith is the assurance that gives present reality to what is hoped for. In the chapter, faith is relational trust in a faithful God who has promised (Heb 11:11) and loyal action that follows: going, offering, refusing, enduring. Luke Timothy Johnson and David deSilva stress that pistis in this setting is close to faithfulness and loyalty. The 'unseen' is not the irrational but the future and heavenly realities God has promised.
misreadings.defence: Traditional commentators broadly agree that 11:1 is not a definition opposing faith to evidence. Some, such as Thomas Schreiner, stress the subjective 'assurance' side more; others, such as Harold Attridge and Craig Koester, stress the objective 'reality' sense of hypostasis. This is a real translation debate, but no serious reading turns faith into belief without reasons; Hebrews grounds faith in God's character and past acts.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Faith as trust in a promise-keeping God, acted on over a lifetime, is both more demanding and more comforting than faith as a feeling of certainty.

misreadings.topic: 'Jesus Christ the same yesterday, today and forever' (Heb 13:8)
misreadings.popular: This verse is often used to argue that because Jesus never changes, every miracle and spiritual gift of the New Testament must be available today in the same way, or more generally as a timeless slogan about God's unchanging nature detached from its setting.
misreadings.inContext: Heb 13:8 sits between a call to remember past leaders who 'spoke the word of God' and whose faith ended well (Heb 13:7) and a warning against 'diverse and strange teachings' about foods (Heb 13:9). The point is that the Jesus those leaders preached is the same Jesus now: do not trade him for new teachings. It echoes the opening of the sermon, where the Son remains while creation changes (Heb 1:10-12; Ps 102:25-27).
misreadings.defence: Those who use the verse for ongoing gifts are not wrong that Christ's character and power are constant, and Pentecostal scholars such as Craig Keener make careful biblical arguments for continuing gifts on other grounds. Cessationists also cite unchanging Christ while denying continuation. Both sides, when careful, agree that 13:8 itself is about fidelity to the original gospel, not a ruling on miracles.
misreadings.whyItMatters: In context the verse is an anchor against drift: the Jesus of the apostles and earlier leaders is enough; we do not need newer, stranger teachings.

misreadings.topic: Shadows and copies: is Hebrews Platonist?
misreadings.popular: Some readers assume Hebrews teaches that the physical world and earthly worship are inferior shadows of a spiritual realm, so what matters is the inner, spiritual life, not bodies, places or rituals.
misreadings.inContext: Hebrews uses words also used by Plato and the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria: 'copy', 'shadow', 'true'. But its main source is Exodus 25:40, where Moses is shown a 'pattern' on the mountain, and its framework is apocalyptic: a heavenly sanctuary, a decisive event in history (Christ's death 'once for all' at the end of the ages, Heb 9:26), a coming world and a future city. Ronald Williamson argued against heavy dependence on Philo; Harold Attridge and Luke Timothy Johnson see real contact with Middle Platonist vocabulary, used in service of a Jewish eschatology. Jesus' body, blood and death in history are essential, not shadows (Heb 10:5-10).
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars such as George Guthrie and Thomas Schreiner generally emphasise the Jewish apocalyptic and typological background and play down Platonism; others, including some Catholic and mainline scholars, see a genuine blend. Nobody serious reads Hebrews as despising the body: the incarnation and suffering of Jesus are central (Heb 2:14-18). The disagreement is about vocabulary and influence, not about whether material life matters.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Hebrews does not offer an escape from history into spirituality. It says the real access to God was opened through a real human life and death and points toward a real future city.

misreadings.topic: The 'rest' of Hebrews 4 as Sunday rules or inner peace only
misreadings.popular: Either the 'Sabbath rest' is used to argue about which day Christians must keep, or it is spiritualised into personal peace and relief from striving at the moment of conversion.
misreadings.inContext: The rest in Hebrews 3-4 draws on Psalm 95, Numbers 14 and Genesis 2:2. It is God's own rest, the promised land seen as a picture of the final inheritance, still future and still to be 'entered' through faithful perseverance (Heb 4:11). Jewish tradition already connected the Sabbath with the world to come; Hebrews uses the rare word sabbatismos (Heb 4:9), Sabbath-celebration, for the joy that awaits God's people. It is both already tasted ('we who have believed do enter', Heb 4:3) and not yet completed.
misreadings.defence: Many evangelical scholars (for example Guthrie and Schreiner) agree the rest is chiefly eschatological, while noting the present tense of 4:3 supports a real present dimension. Debates over the Christian Sabbath are legitimate but draw on other texts; Hebrews 4 is not their main battleground.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The passage keeps hope forward-looking: believers are still a pilgrim people who must not stop short of the land, like their ancestors at Kadesh.

misreadings.topic: Jesus' sacrifice as only a legal transaction
misreadings.popular: Hebrews shows that God's wrath required blood, so Jesus paid the penalty; the high-priest language is mainly a picture of a legal debt being cancelled so individuals can go to heaven.
misreadings.inContext: Hebrews' main picture is not the law court but the sanctuary: Yom Kippur purification so that a holy God can dwell among an unclean people and they can 'draw near'. Blood in Leviticus is life given to cleanse and consecrate (Lev 17:11). The aim is a cleansed conscience, open access and a covenant people who worship (Heb 9:14; Heb 10:19-22). Jesus is also a priest who sympathises and intercedes now (Heb 7:25). Craig Koester and David Moffitt emphasise that in Hebrews atonement includes Jesus' ascension into God's presence, not only his death.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars such as Schreiner and Guthrie affirm penal substitution as part of the New Testament picture (Heb 9:28 echoes Isa 53:12, 'to bear the sins of many'), and the warnings about judgment show God's justice is real. They agree that Hebrews' distinctive emphasis is priestly and relational access, and that a purely transactional preaching of the cross is thinner than the text.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The goal of the sacrifice in Hebrews is relationship: bold, clean-hearted approach to God within a worshipping community.

perspectives.name: Supersessionist (replacement) reading
perspectives.who: Much of the patristic and medieval tradition, for example John Chrysostom's homilies on Hebrews, and many later popular readers.
perspectives.summary: Hebrews proves that the old covenant and its people have been replaced. The Jewish religion is a set of obsolete shadows; the church is the new Israel and inherits all its promises.
perspectives.strengths: It takes seriously the sharp language of Hebrews ('obsolete', Heb 8:13; 'he takes away the first', Heb 10:9) and the claim that there is no other sacrifice for sin. It recognises how central Christ's finality is to the book.
perspectives.critiques: Hebrews never mentions 'the Jews' as a group, never rejects the Jewish people, and calls Israel's saints 'our' fathers. The new covenant it celebrates is promised to Israel and Judah. It reads later Jewish-Christian hostility back into an intra-Jewish sermon, and it has a tragic history of fuelling contempt.

perspectives.name: Fulfilment and continuity
perspectives.who: Mainstream evangelical and Catholic commentators, for example F. F. Bruce, George Guthrie, Craig Koester, Thomas Schreiner.
perspectives.summary: One story, one God, one people of faith across the ages. The Levitical system was God's good provision, pointing to a fuller reality; with Christ that fuller reality has come, so the earlier means of access is completed and set aside, but the promises to Israel are kept, not cancelled.
perspectives.strengths: It fits the 'many times and many ways' opening, the typological reading of the tabernacle, and the inclusion of Israel's saints in the people of faith (Heb 11:39-40).
perspectives.critiques: Jewish and post-Holocaust readers ask whether 'fulfilment' still implies that Judaism today is empty. Others note it can underplay the genuine discontinuity Hebrews asserts, or alternatively soften the sharpness of the warnings.

perspectives.name: Jewish-Christian intramural debate (new or renewed covenantalism)
perspectives.who: Richard Hays, Mark Nanos, Pamela Eisenbaum, and in different ways Luke Timothy Johnson.
perspectives.summary: Hebrews comes from inside first-century Judaism before 'Judaism' and 'Christianity' were separate religions. Like the Qumran community, which also saw itself as the people of the new covenant, the author argues about the right way to be faithful to Israel's God, now through Messiah Jesus. Hays calls it Jewish sectarian 'new covenantalism'; Nanos prefers 'renewed covenantalism'.
perspectives.strengths: It matches the book's total immersion in Jewish Scripture and worship, its silence about Gentile-Jewish tension, and its historical setting in the decades before the parting of the ways.
perspectives.critiques: Critics say it can blur the real newness Hebrews claims for Jesus' once-for-all sacrifice, and that a sect claiming the old system is 'near vanishing' is still making exclusive claims that later readers will hear as replacement. Some note that the audience may have included many Gentiles.

perspectives.name: Platonic and Philonic background
perspectives.who: Older scholars such as James Moffatt and Ceslas Spicq, and with nuance Harold Attridge and James Thompson.
perspectives.summary: Hebrews thinks in the categories of Alexandrian Jewish philosophy: the heavenly, true and eternal versus the earthly, copied and passing. Its affinity with Philo of Alexandria suggests an author like Apollos, an Alexandrian Jew.
perspectives.strengths: It explains vocabulary such as 'shadow', 'copy' and 'true tabernacle' and the polished Greek rhetoric of the book.
perspectives.critiques: Ronald Williamson and others showed the differences from Philo are deep: Hebrews has a decisive historical event, an end of the ages and a coming city. Shared vocabulary does not mean shared worldview.

perspectives.name: Apocalyptic and Second Temple background
perspectives.who: C. K. Barrett, Lincoln Hurst, David Moffitt, and many recent commentators.
perspectives.summary: The two-level picture of Hebrews is Jewish apocalyptic: a heavenly temple where God is enthroned (as in 1 Enoch, Daniel and the Qumran Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice), two ages, and a coming kingdom that cannot be shaken. Melchizedek speculation like 11QMelchizedek belongs here too.
perspectives.strengths: It accounts for the future orientation of the book (the 'coming world', Heb 2:5; the 'city to come', Heb 13:14) and the emphasis on resurrection and ascension.
perspectives.critiques: Hebrews does use philosophical vocabulary, and many scholars think the either-or is false: a Hellenistic Jewish preacher could blend apocalyptic structure with Platonist language.

keyTerms.inContext: Used about thirteen times to compare what God gave earlier with what he gives in the Son: better hope, covenant, promises, sacrifices, possession, country, resurrection. It is a comparison of good and better within one plan.

To bring to completion or goal; in priestly use, to consecrate for service. Jesus was 'made perfect through sufferings' (qualified as priest), and the law could not 'perfect' worshippers, that is, bring them fully into God's presence.
A broker or guarantor who stands between two parties. In a patronage society, the mediator brings clients near to a great patron. Jesus mediates a better covenant and guarantees it with his life.
The Septuagint word for berit, God's binding relational commitment to a people. In 9:16-17 the author plays on its other meaning, a will that takes effect at death.

keyTerms.usual: Belief in doctrines, or certainty without evidence.
keyTerms.inContext: Trust, loyalty and faithfulness toward a faithful God, shown over time in obedience and endurance. Jesus is the 'pioneer and perfecter' of this faith.
Underlying reality or substance (the Son is the 'exact imprint of his hypostasis', Heb 1:3), also firm confidence. Faith gives present reality to what is hoped for.
A leader who goes first and opens the way for others to follow, like a trailblazer or the founder of a city. Jesus leads 'many sons and daughters to glory' through suffering.
One who runs ahead and enters first so others can follow; Jesus has gone 'behind the curtain' as forerunner, anchoring the hope of those who come after.
Decisively and unrepeatably. Contrasts with the yearly Yom Kippur rite and the daily offerings; Christ's self-offering does not need repeating.
God's own rest and the promised inheritance; sabbatismos (perhaps coined) suggests the festive Sabbath celebration of the world to come.
Drawn from Exodus 25:40: what Moses built followed a heavenly pattern. A shadow is real and points to its source; the earthly sanctuary was a true, God-given sketch of the heavenly reality.
In the Greek city, the free citizen's right to speak openly; here the right of access to God's presence and the courage to confess Jesus publicly despite shame.
Public loss of honour in a society built on reputation. Hebrews treats sharing Christ's reproach as honour in God's court.
A synagogue-style sermon that both encourages and urges. The same phrase is used for Paul's synagogue address in Acts 13:15.
